title: Criminal Appeals & Bail Pending Appeal (Suspension of Sentence) — Bombay High Court
content:
In short

A person convicted by a Sessions Court can appeal to the Bombay High Court under Section 415 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). Along with the appeal, the High Court can be asked to suspend the sentence and release the appellant on bail while the appeal is decided (Section 430 BNSS). Appeals against conviction to the High Court generally have to be filed within 60 days of the judgment; delay can be condoned only for sufficient cause.

When an appeal lies, and to which court

  • Conviction by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge — appeal to the High Court.
  • Conviction by a Magistrate — appeal ordinarily to the Sessions Court.
  • Acquittal — the State (and, in some cases, the victim) may appeal; the accused should be represented from the first hearing.
  • Where no appeal lies, a revision (Sections 438–442 BNSS) may be available against a legally flawed order.

Suspension of sentence and bail pending appeal

Criminal appeals in the High Court can take years to be heard finally. Suspension of sentence decides whether the appellant waits in jail or outside. Courts commonly look at:

  • the length of the sentence and how much has already been served;
  • whether there are arguable points in the appeal — for example, contradictions in eyewitness evidence, a weak recovery, or a role different from co-accused;
  • conduct while on bail during trial, and the likelihood of the appeal being heard soon;
  • for life sentences, courts examine the record more closely and suspension is less readily granted.

Our reported orders page has short notes on how the Bombay High Court has applied these principles, including an order where bail pending appeal was refused.

What the appeal involves

  1. Certified copies of the judgment and the trial record (depositions, exhibits) are obtained.
  2. Grounds of appeal are drafted from the evidence actually recorded at trial.
  3. The appeal and the application for suspension of sentence are filed together in the Bombay High Court, Mumbai.
  4. The suspension application is argued on its own merits; the appeal is later heard finally on the full record.
  5. If the sentence is suspended, the appellant is released on bail with conditions set by the court.

Documents to bring to the first meeting

  • Copy of the Sessions Court judgment and order on sentence
  • Charge-sheet and, if available, the depositions of witnesses
  • Details of custody — date of arrest, periods on bail, date of conviction
  • Any earlier bail orders in the case

Related

  • Bail applications
  • Sessions trial defence
  • How murder cases are defended

Bail pending appeal: what it means

Bail pending appeal (also called bail after conviction) means the appellate court suspends the sentence and releases the convicted person on bail until the appeal is decided. The conviction itself remains. This is different from bail pending trial, where the accused is presumed innocent: after conviction, the court looks mainly at whether the appeal raises arguable points and how long the appellant would otherwise spend in custody before it is heard.

How long does a bail-pending-appeal application take?

The application is filed with the appeal and listed for hearing after notice to the State. The time to a hearing depends on the court’s board. For shorter fixed-term sentences, suspension is often considered at the admission stage itself; for life sentences, the court usually examines the trial record closely before deciding. Long custody already undergone is a recognised reason to seek early listing.

Appeal against conviction by a Magistrate (Sessions Court, Pune)

Convictions by a Judicial Magistrate are ordinarily appealed to the Sessions Court. This includes cheque-bounce (Section 138 NI Act) cases, where the appellate court may direct a deposit of at least 20% of the fine or compensation under Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act while suspending the sentence.

This page explains the law in general terms. Every matter turns on its own facts — please speak to an advocate about yours.
